text: The abstract scan hypothesis has a category error. Q provides theoretical mechanism design results (BIC, IIR, WBB mechanisms with constant-factor GFT approximation to first-best). P studies whether LLM agents can negotiate contracts that improve cooperation in a spatial-temporal game. These do not integrate cleanly: (1) Qs mechanisms require specific payment rules and allocation rules that satisfy incentive constraints - Ps contract framework does not implement mechanism design, it tests whether agents can negotiate binding agreements. (2) Q assumes independent private values/costs and analyzes equilibrium behavior under truthfulness; P tests bounded-rational LLM behavior in negotiation without mechanism constraints. (3) The claim LLMs could empirically achieve Qs theoretical guarantees conflates mechanism execution (agents report types, mechanism computes outcome) with contract negotiation (agents bargain over terms). If anything, the question should be: do LLM agents playing Qs mechanism behave truthfully enough that the approximation holds? But Ps infrastructure does not test mechanism implementation - it tests contract formation.

The abstract scan hypothesis conflates distinct frameworks. P studies agents negotiating contracts AS the cooperation mechanism in a spatial-temporal game (CT). Q provides a theoretical mechanism with specific incentive constraints (BIC, IIR, WBB). For the hypothesis to work: (1) P contract framework must be able to express Q mechanism structure, (2) LLM negotiation must converge on Q mechanism terms, (3) enforcement must maintain Q incentive properties. P abstract mentions "contract representations from formal/code to natural language" but does not claim infrastructure for implementing arbitrary mechanism designs. The gap is not "adaptation" but whether P framework can express Q mechanism at all.

Alternative direction: Compare mechanism design vs contract negotiation for multidimensional bilateral trade. Q shows simple mechanisms achieve constant-factor first-best GFT under BIC/IIR/WBB. P shows LLM agents with self-negotiated contracts exceed cooperation without contracts. Research question: In a multidimensional bilateral trade environment (one XOS buyer, one additive seller), do LLM agents using Ps contract negotiation framework achieve comparable GFT to Qs theoretical mechanism? This tests whether flexible contract-based cooperation can match rigid mechanism design under bounded rationality. Contribution would be empirical comparison of two paradigms, not validation of Qs guarantees. Feasibility concern: need to operationalize XOS valuations and additive costs in an environment LLMs can navigate (like Ps CT game but with trade structure). Gain: moderate - shows whether contract flexibility compensates for lack of incentive guarantees.

Reframed hypothesis: The genuine question is whether contract-negotiating LLM agents (P) in multidimensional bilateral trade settings (Q) can EMERGE mechanism-like behavior that approximates Q theoretical bounds. This is not "implementing Q mechanism" but testing if LLM negotiation discovers efficient trade rules. Contribution would be: (1) empirical GFT measurements under LLM bargaining vs Q theoretical bounds, (2) analysis of what contract structures emerge, (3) whether contract enforcement (P contribution) enables outcomes closer to first-best than unenforced negotiation. This requires building experimental environment combining Q valuation structures (XOS buyer, additive seller) with P contract negotiation protocol.

Technical clarification on Q vs P frameworks: Q uses standard mechanism design - agents report types to a central mechanism that computes allocation/payments via fixed rules. The mechanism designer controls the outcome function. P uses decentralized contract negotiation - agents bargain over terms, then contracts are enforced. These are architecturally different: mechanism design assumes agents cannot commit to strategies beyond reporting; contract framework assumes agents can commit to future actions via enforcement. The reframed hypothesis (ledger #4) correctly shifts from "implementing Q mechanism" to "can LLM contract negotiation approximate Q GFT bounds." This is empirically testable: build bilateral trade environment with XOS buyer/additive seller valuations, let LLMs negotiate contracts, measure GFT vs Q theoretical constant-factor bound. Key prediction: if LLMs discover mechanism-like terms (e.g., "report values, split surplus per rule X"), contracts should approximate Q bounds; if they bargain directly over trades, may exceed or fall short depending on negotiation skill.
